title: Is perfect matching in general graphs in deterministic NC?
formal: Do there exist constants C,a,b>0 and a logspace-uniform family of Boolean circuits which, on the adjacency matrix of every n-vertex simple undirected graph, output a perfect matching or correctly report that none exists, with at most C(n+2)^a gates and depth at most C(log₂(n+2))^b?
context:
A polynomial-time sequential algorithm is known, so the open issue is the length of the dependency chain after work is spread across many processors. Following one augmenting path after another does not automatically give a polylogarithmic number of parallel steps. The processor bound matters too: solving many possibilities simultaneously is useful only if the total work remains polynomial.

Choosing matching edges independently is dangerous. On a four-cycle, every edge can be excluded while preserving some perfect matching. Removing all four edges at once nevertheless destroys every solution. A parallel construction must coordinate its choices around one compatible matching rather than around separate existence certificates.

General graphs also need more structure than the bipartite case. Two disjoint triangles have an even total number of vertices and admit a fractional assignment of one half to every edge, giving total incident weight one at each vertex. They have no perfect matching. This example shows why degree constraints alone do not describe the general matching polytope; odd vertex sets impose additional conditions.

The June 2026 bipartite result is a major nearby advance. Its theorem covers bipartite graphs, including polynomially bounded weights. The present card deliberately asks for arbitrary graphs, where the deterministic polynomial-processor target remains unresolved in the checked literature.
why: I include this because perfect matching is a basic polynomial-time graph problem for which randomization and parallelism interact in a particularly sharp way. The question asks whether randomness is needed to find globally compatible choices quickly, and whether the structural tools for odd cycles can be made as parallel as the algebraic ones.
definitions: The input is the n×n binary adjacency matrix of a graph on [n], with symmetry and zero diagonal promised. A perfect matching is a set of edges with exactly one edge incident to each vertex. Output is a flag and an n×n binary incidence matrix for the chosen matching; when the flag reports nonexistence the remaining output bits are ignored. The empty graph has the empty perfect matching. Circuits use fan-in-two AND/OR, fan-in-one NOT, constants 0,1 and unrestricted fan-out. Depth counts gates on the longest input-output path and size counts gates; the n² output positions are specified as part of the description. A deterministic Turing transducer on unary input 1^n writes the description using O(log₂(n+2)) work bits, with read-only input and write-only output. Constants and generator are fixed across n; every valid input must receive an exact answer. No randomness, oracle, advice, bipartiteness or other structural graph promise is supplied.

progress.text: The randomized parallel approach of Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani uses isolation to single out a matching. Svensson and Tarnawski review this starting point and the need to derandomize it.

Svensson and Tarnawski give a deterministic general-graph algorithm in $O(\log^3 n)$ parallel time with $n^{O(\log^2 n)}$ processors. It achieves quasi-NC, leaving a quasipolynomial-versus-polynomial resource gap.
Chatterjee, Ghosh, Gurjar, Raj, and Thierauf prove an NC result for bipartite matching. This new preprint does not state the general-graph theorem sought here.

answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

importance.reason: A canonical deterministic parallel-algorithm and derandomization question for a basic graph optimization problem.

sentences: Perfect matching seeks pairwise disjoint edges that cover every vertex of a graph.
The question asks for a deterministic parallel algorithm on general graphs with polynomially many processors and polylogarithmic running time.
Sequential polynomial-time algorithms do not supply this bound because their matching updates may depend on earlier choices.
General graphs also contain odd cycles, which require coordination beyond the constraints that suffice in bipartite graphs.
The saved card distinguishes this target from the nearby bipartite advance and asks whether compatible matching decisions can be organized efficiently in parallel without randomness.
